[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This facility is one of many individual buildings that make up Amazon Web Services Ohio data center campus, spanning Franklin, Licking, and Union counties and centered on New Albany, a suburb of Columbus that has become one of the most significant data center economic development stories in the Midwest. Ohio hosts AWS us-east-2 cloud region. The City of New Albany own published materials, along with CoStar, DataCenterDynamics, Data Center Frontier, and local television and news outlets including 10TV and NBC4, document a series of AWS investment announcements in the area, including a 3.5 billion dollar, five building campus expansion, an earlier 7.8 billion dollar investment reported in 2023, and city and county economic development materials describing a combined multi billion dollar footprint that the City of New Albany credits with contributing 1.4 billion dollars to Licking County gross domestic product. New Albany city council approved a 30 year local tax abatement to support the continued buildout. Some buildings in this campus carry community assigned tracking codenames such as CMH50, CMH53, CMH56, CMH59, and CMH62, referencing the Columbus airport code, which data center trend tracking sites use to distinguish buildings from satellite imagery and permitting records, though these are not AWS own official building designations. AWS does not publish individual building addresses, capacities, or specifications, so this specific building construction date, square footage, and critical IT megawattage cannot be independently confirmed from any AWS owned source, even though the broader New Albany area campus and its economic impact are extensively documented in government and trade press.

profile.disclosure_policy: Confirmed directly on AWS own Global Infrastructure page (aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/): AWS does not publish specific street addresses or per-building technical specifications (square footage, power capacity in MW) for its data centers, as a matter of stated security and operational policy. AWS states each Region consists of a minimum of three isolated, physically separate Availability Zones, each with independent power, cooling, and physical security, but does not break this down to individual facility addresses. This session confirmed this disclosure policy directly rather than assuming it, and applies this finding to AWS records that otherwise have no facility specific address, square footage, planned capacity, or critical_it_mw on file. This is a company wide policy finding, not a statement that no such facility exists at this location.

reading.body:
AWS CMH59 is one building in Amazon's Ohio data center campus spanning three counties around New Albany, a Columbus suburb that has become a major Midwest AI infrastructure site. AWS does not publish individual building specifications, so this facility's power capacity and rack density cannot be confirmed from the operator itself; one industry index estimates the entire regional us-east-2 campus at approximately 500 MW operational capacity, though AWS does not independently confirm this figure. The broader New Albany area has drawn documented investment commitments exceeding $11 billion from AWS since 2023, supported by a 30-year local tax abatement, making the campus economically significant to Licking County.

Ohio ranks ninth among states in published data center capacity at 60.4 MW across eight facilities with disclosed specifications, though 76 facilities are mapped in the state and most publish no figures. CMH59 sits within the largest undisclosed capacity footprint in Ohio, the AWS us-east-2 region that hosts one of the company's primary cloud delivery points for the eastern United States.

Whether this campus matters to AI scaling depends on whether the estimated 500 MW regional figure and announced continued expansion translate into published specifications. Until AWS discloses per-facility power consumption and utilization, this building's contribution to US AI compute capacity remains opaque despite its documented economic footprint and role in a region positioned as a major cloud infrastructure hub.
